camera.note: held by a second person; subject framed well between 20-30s, 100-110s and 120-125s

scan.method: 1 fps sweep over all 127s, then 15 fps bursts on candidate moments

events.cues: upright, small steps, arms low; no clear stroke extension
rotates to the right, arms swing wide for balance, feet stay on the ice
faces camera, travels forward; feet open to a wide V then draw back together, repeated; arms come out wide at 103.3-103.5 for balance; knees only lightly bent
events.coaching: deeper knee bend and heels pressing out would make the lemons rounder; arms should stay steady at waist height rather than flying out

events.cues: clearest example in the clip: 3-4 open/close cycles traveling toward the camera, feet symmetric, upper body quiet, hands held in front
events.coaching: good symmetry; push out through the heels and bend the knees more to widen each lemon

observations: Best clip so far: 4K, and the subject reaches 40-60% of frame height in three windows.
Camera is held by another person and often points at the operator's shirt or at other skaters; roughly 25% of the clip is blocked or off-subject.
Busy public session: 10+ skaters, several children with training aids, which is the hardest case for automatic tracking.
Two clean swizzle sequences are the first genuinely labelable skill attempts in the whole batch.
verdict: Two usable swizzle examples. Framing works when the camera stays on the skater; the loss is from pointing away, not from settings.
